text: The crash was a deliberate disposal burn. After completing its survey, Cassini would have to be gotten out of the way so it wouldn't drift into or fall on Saturn's moons. The main concern was trace contamination: even a spacecraft that has been in the solar system for decades can carry microbes, dust, and organic compounds of terrestrial origin. Saturn's moons, especially Enceladus and Titan, are considered potentially habitable, so you don't want to leave a spacecraft sitting on their surfaces. By plunging into the atmosphere and burning up, the craft is destroyed before it can contact a moon. That's why the end-of-mission maneuver was a dive into Saturn.

It’s usually a matter of stance and how the board’s weight is distributed. When you push with one leg, the other leg—the one that stays on the board—has to hold your weight while you’re moving. If your back foot is planted too far back or angled outward, the ankle and knee are doing a lot of stabilizing work, which causes that ache. The pushing leg extends and bends in a rhythmic way, but the stationary leg is often locked into an isometric hold. Muscles that hold a fixed position for a long time tire out differently than ones that are moving, and that fatigue can show up as a dull pain in the shin, knee, or ankle.

I’d check your foot position first. If you’re a regular, your back foot should be near the tail, but not so far back that it sticks out beyond the board’s edge. If it’s too far back, your center of mass shifts and you’re leaning backward to compensate, which strains the knee ligaments. If you’re a goofy, it’s the same idea, just mirrored. A common mistake is pointing that foot straight back or angled out too much; keep it closer to parallel with the board, maybe with the toe slightly turned in for stability.

Also consider the impact. When you land from a drop or ride over a crack, the stationary leg absorbs a lot of force because it’s the primary contact point. If your stance is too wide or too narrow, that impact travels straight up the leg, hurting the knee or hip. A slightly narrower stance often helps distribute the load better. If the pain is sharp rather than a dull ache, it might be a sign that you’re overusing a joint, so adjusting your foot placement and taking breaks between sessions can make a difference. The goal is to find a balance where your stationary leg feels supported without being locked in a rigid position, and to make sure your weight isn’t shifted too far toward that foot.

The term “Afro-American” isn’t a claim about where Black Americans live or what their nationality is. It’s a reminder that the Black population in the US grew mostly from enslaved people brought over from West and Central Africa. Not every Black person today can point to a modern African border as their family’s origin; the label is about descent, not residence. I’ve noticed people treat “Afro-American” and “African-American” as the same thing, and in casual usage they often are, but strictly they’re distinct. “African-American” can mean someone with an American identity plus African roots, or a direct link to Africa. “Afro-American” is narrower: an African descent identity. It was not the everyday name for Black people in the 18th or 19th centuries; those groups often had their own names, and the label is more of a later, scholarly or political shorthand. So the word does not mean most Black Americans currently live in Africa, or that everyone’s family comes from a specific modern country. It names the African source population that formed the basis of the Black community in the US. That’s the connection the term points to. The overlap is why the two labels get blurred in everyday talk.

Most of the heavy hardware initially came from seized Syrian army depots, but the state supply lines kept the government equipped. The Tehran-Damascus axis, operating through Hezbollah, brought in quantities of RPGs and mortars. Cross-border smuggling from Iraq and Turkey filled the gaps for opposition fighters. They still get them because the conflict has not resolved into a clear victory. The state continues its reliance on Iranian and Russian backing, while rebels maintain a constant need to replace losses. It is less about finding new sources and more about keeping the pipeline open to survive a prolonged stalemate.

Most of the time the problem is that the same receptor that makes you feel euphoric is also the receptor that drives tolerance, withdrawal, and the other effects you are bothered by. You cannot cleanly switch off one set of consequences while keeping the other. Opioids hit mu receptors and give that rush, but they also change how much drug you need over time and what happens when you stop; stimulant like cocaine act through dopamine pathways and give the high, but they also drive craving, and after-peak effects like anxiety or sleep disruption. That is not a design flaw someone can engineer away; it is what the systems do.

Another thing that makes “zero adverse effects” harder than it sounds is that dose-response curves are not perfectly linear. There is a threshold, and a maximum effect where more drug does not add much. But there are also dose ranges where adverse effects start to dominate. So the same molecule that gives a good effect at one dose can be uncomfortable or harmful at a higher dose. A drug that only ever gives pleasant feelings at the therapeutic range, and only ever adverse effects outside it, would be a real advance, but the separation is usually less clean than you hope.

Tolerance makes the “bad” part harder to miss. After some use, the baseline shifts. You need more to get the same effect, and stopping produces a deficit that feels very unpleasant. For some drugs the withdrawal is mostly miserable rather than dangerous, but miserable is still an adverse effect.

I also think part of the answer is that the body resists being pushed far from its normal state. Strong positive reinforcement triggers the same systems that, when the stimulus stops, feel like a loss. That is the core of dependency: the brain learns that a state is achievable and then resents the baseline when it is not. So a drug with intense euphoria but no downsides would have to give the high without the brain treating it as something to seek out or lose, and that combination is hard to maintain.

There are examples of drugs that are useful precisely because they do not have the classic euphoria-then-withdrawal problem, but the ones that are euphoric tend to come with a tradeoff somewhere in the body’s reaction. As far as I know, nobody has made a drug that reliably gives intense pleasure with genuinely zero adverse effects, and the pharmacology makes that a strange target.

Hi there,

What you're describing is probably not a normal headache, so don't just shrug it off. A long shopping day stacks up in ways that don't show up until you're exhausted: too little food and fluid, too much walking and standing, plus the mental load of keeping track of choices. That can produce a different kind of pain, often pressure or aching in the head or shoulders. It's real, and it's a sign of cumulative stress and fatigue, not a sign that you're imagining it.

If it keeps coming back, see a doctor to rule out eye or sinus problems.

That milk answer is a good example of semantic priming. Cows and milk are so strongly tied together in everyday knowledge that, when you were asked what cows drink, your mind grabbed the most available association instead of checking the literal fact. Saying silk five times probably put you in a low-effort, repetitive state, which makes automatic associations surface more easily. The question is also a bit of a trick, because most people think of cows as dairy producers. Your brother's repetition likely reduced working memory load, so you did not re-check the question. In at least the US, cow and milk are culturally hard-wired, and one slip after priming is normal. If you keep doing this across unrelated topics, a quick doctor check is reasonable. As far as I know, this kind of priming is common in adults; one odd answer after repetition is not a cognitive red flag.

I don't have your specific questions in front of me, but the usual house-buying issues are mortgage pre-approval, seller disclosures, appraisal, title search, home inspection, and negotiating repairs. In most cases, get a pre-approval letter before you start looking; without it you won't be taken seriously. Ask the seller for disclosure statements, and read them carefully. At the offer stage, leave room for a contingency for inspection and appraisal. If the inspection finds problems, you can ask the seller to repair or reduce the price, but don't assume every minor issue is worth fighting over. Title search usually comes from your lawyer or a title company, and it can surface liens or ownership problems that make you rethink the purchase. The biggest risk is that the home's value at appraisal comes in under the agreed price, which may require a new price or renegotiation. I'm not a lawyer, but for contracts and closing, use a local attorney or real estate agent, and read the fine print. If you send me the exact questions, I can answer them directly rather than guessing at what you're worried about. I'll keep this short. Send them whenever.

Cheers,

The main difference is formulation. A 3-in-1 is usually one all-purpose surfactant blend intended for skin and hair, while separate products are designed for one job each. Bodywash typically uses milder surfactants for skin and sometimes moisturizers; shampoo targets hair with stronger cleaning agents and, in 2-in-1 products, a small amount of conditioner or silicone-like conditioners. A true 3-in-1 has to balance all of those roles in one bottle. That means it will generally clean hair less aggressively and moisturize skin less intensely than dedicated products. It also tends to be more concentrated and more alkaline than skin products, which can leave hair rough or scalp dry if you are using a true shampoo in the same bottle. The tradeoff is convenience over specificity. For my own use, I'd pick the separate products if I can; the 3-in-1 works well when the routine has to be short and the space small. If the label does not say what it actually contains, assume it is a compromise. For me, it worked well enough for a short rinse, though my hair felt a bit waxy and my skin needed extra lotion. I would still keep separate products at home.

They mainly use satellite-based geodesy, because the movement is tiny: centimetres or less per year, so ordinary surveying is too coarse. The standard method is GPS/GNSS. A continent is not measured as one point; networks of fixed reference stations are distributed across the plate. Each station records its position repeatedly, and comparing positions at two times gives a velocity vector for that station. Those velocities are expressed relative to a global reference frame, and the plate motion is modeled. In addition, scientists combine GPS with satellite laser ranging, very long baseline interferometry, and InSAR for surface deformation. Typical speeds are tens of millimetres per year, which struck me as odd, but they add up quickly over millions of years. Older geologic evidence, such as seafloor magnetic stripes, gives long-term plate motion, but for present-day speed, geodetic measurements are the direct way. Public GNSS velocity maps from geodesy groups show each station's motion relative to a chosen reference frame. Different choices of reference frame change the numbers by a few millimetres per year, so the reported speed depends partly on which frame is picked. The physical motion is the same; the coordinate description isn't.

Inbreeding raises homozygosity across the genome, so offspring are much more likely to inherit two copies of rare recessive alleles. Many genes affecting cognition are polygenic, and the damaging variants are usually rare, so in a randomly mating population they're typically masked by a normal allele. Close relatives share more of those variants, and when they have children, the chance of homozygous recessive genotypes at many of these loci goes up. That's the basic mechanism behind inbreeding depression, and it applies to IQ.

Human studies don't show a dramatic collapse in IQ; the reported deficit is modest, on the order of a few points, though it's statistically real. The effect scales with the degree of relatedness, so first-cousin offspring are affected more than, say, offspring of second cousins. It isn't that inbreeding creates new mutations; it mostly uncovers recessive load that was already there.

Pain is the brain’s interpretation of injury signals, not a fixed number attached to a body part. In most everyday injuries, a limb wound is not usually a medical emergency, so the brain has less reason to treat it as one. An arm wound may feel less severe because a limb is easier to guard, is usually clothed, and is less likely to involve vital organs, so there is less urgency in how the brain reads it. Soft tissue padding in the forearm and shoulder can also blunt the signal. People often pay more attention to wounds in areas they notice or value; the brain can reduce perceived pain when the injury does not look immediately life-threatening. That said, arm injuries are not automatically milder. A clean cut on the palm or a broken wrist can be quite painful. The perceived difference is mostly about context, attention, and lower risk, not a special immunity of the arm.

Carbon monoxide is far more dangerous to breathe than carbon dioxide because of what it does to hemoglobin. Red blood cells carry oxygen bound to hemoglobin, and that binding has to be fast enough to keep up with the heart's pumping rate. Carbon monoxide binds to the same site on hemoglobin with an affinity roughly two hundred times that of oxygen, so even small amounts of CO in the air gradually displace the oxygen that hemoglobin would otherwise pick up in the lungs. The result is a functional reduction in oxygen-carrying capacity, and the body effectively suffocates while the lungs themselves may be perfectly healthy. This is the carboxyhemoglobin pathway: CO binds hemoglobin and holds it there for a long time, so each breath introduces more CO while the oxygen that hemoglobin would carry is displaced.

Carbon dioxide does not share that trap. It is a normal metabolic byproduct that the body produces continuously, and the lungs are built to exhale it efficiently. At everyday concentrations it is harmless; in most cases CO2 becomes a problem only at concentrations well above what normal room air contains, where it can cause drowsiness and headaches. The danger of CO lies in that strong, long-lived binding to hemoglobin, rather than direct irritation of the airways. A person breathing normal air is constantly producing CO2 and clearing it, so CO2 is not generally treated as a poison, whereas CO can be harmful even at low partial pressures.

As far as I know, the practical difference is this: CO2 is the waste your body is already managing; CO is an intruder that sticks to the oxygen carrier and keeps it from doing its job. That is why even mild CO exposure can be dangerous, while breathing a higher share of CO2 is tolerated up to fairly high levels.

The brace position is a defensive posture used just before impact. In most emergency procedures it means keeping your feet flat and gripping the floor, leaning your body forward, and holding onto a fixed part of the aircraft. The position keeps your body compact and limits how far your head and torso can travel if the plane is hit hard. When an aircraft stops or descends suddenly, loose objects can become projectiles. If you are upright and unsupported, your body tends to strike seats, panels, or the floor. By bracing, you absorb part of the motion through your own muscles and posture, which can reduce the severity of injuries to the neck, chest, and head. It also helps you stay connected to the seatbelt or a fixed point. It will not guarantee a safe outcome; it lowers the chances of being thrown around and cut by cabin fittings.

For a new colleague, the practical point is that bracing is about controlling your own movement, not waiting for someone else to tell you exactly which body part to move. If an emergency is imminent, get into that posture, keep it until cleared, and do not improvise based on movies or older advice such as covering your head with your arms.

The premise is mostly a matter of continuity, not absence. Old businesses did exist before industrialization, but many were small workshops, family firms, or local trading houses, and their legal identity often changed when ownership or name shifted. A company that keeps the same business name and operations can look ancient, but the original owners, structure, and location usually do not remain the same. That makes the current brand a descendant of an older trade rather than the unbroken original. As a result, very few pre-industrial firms survive intact and stay well known under the same identity.

I used to think a low-rate dealer loan was the obvious choice. Then I started comparing actual total cost rather than the headline rate. My position is simple: a bank loan can be cheaper than a dealership loan because dealers sell the financing package, not just the interest rate. A dealership may advertise a low nominal rate, but the payment you sign includes dealer fees and add-ons like extended service or paint protection, and sometimes a trade-in offset built into the deal. The bank does not sell you a bundle of extras. You take a loan for a named amount and a term; the cost is easier to audit. That matters because dealerships have every incentive to add value-added products; those are where the profit often comes from, and they can make a low rate feel more expensive than a slightly higher bank rate.

This has changed how I buy vehicles. When I compare offers, I look at the payment for the same term and the total of payments plus any dealer add-ons. If a dealership quote includes a lower interest rate but also includes an extended warranty and a service plan, the monthly payment may be the same or higher than a plain bank loan. A bank quote is usually just principal and interest over a term; you choose extras. That control is the real advantage. This means a bank can beat the effective cost even at a higher rate, with no dealer extras pulling the price up.

Sometimes a dealer's low rate is a true automaker-funded discount. But in my experience the advertised rate is the easiest hook. The total package is what determines cost. If the bank quote is lower after stripping out dealer add-ons, the bank is the cheaper path regardless of nominal rate. That has made me treat any low-rate dealer offer with suspicion and ask for a line-item breakdown before trusting the number on the page.

I think this is why people are confused. A dealership can show a lower APR and still make you pay more in fees and add-ons, while a bank's slightly higher APR is offset by a slimmer cost structure. The lesson I carry around is that financing a car is not a single-interest-rate comparison. It is a comparison of total outlay, and in many deals the bank wins on that basis. That has made me slower to jump on the shiny low-rate offer.

For me the interesting thing is not that recreational marijuana is legal in most states, but how uneven that is in practice; as far as I know, 19 states and the District of Columbia have legalized adult-use cannabis, but only some of those let you grow a small number of plants at home, and the rules on where you can smoke it in public vary a lot. In the US, at least, legality on the state level does not settle federal law, so someone who lives in a legal state can still face problems crossing state lines. I also think the tax situation is one of the stranger corners: states may levy excise taxes, but the federal business tax code makes it hard for cannabis companies to deduct ordinary costs, which keeps prices higher than the market would suggest. My position is that state legalization is broadly good, with one caveat: the patchwork of rules makes interstate travel and business messy.

I keep hearing that the body "produces electricity," which is misleading. It isn't a battery. What it does is maintain voltage differences across cell membranes using ion gradients, mostly sodium, potassium, chloride and calcium. The sodium-potassium pump keeps those gradients going, and neurons fire when voltage-gated channels open. In most cases the effect is tiny: microvolts to millivolts. It strikes me as odd that people talk about it as if the body is generating current like a generator. It isn't. It's electrochemistry, not a power source. In my view the word "electricity" does a lot of heavy lifting in the question.

There is a common misunderstanding that sampling is lazy borrowing, but I think the opposite is true: sampling is editing an older recording into a new musical argument. In most hip-hop and electronic production, the sampler isn't just copying a phrase. They are deciding what part of the old record to keep, and what to throw away, and how to make it fit the new song.

For me, the interesting part is the technical process. A producer might pull a short loop into a digital audio workstation, chop it into slices, and rearrange them. They may stretch or compress tempo, shift pitch, filter muddy frequencies, and change the rhythm. A four-bar loop from an old soul track can become a beat when broken into smaller pieces. That is why two samples can sound different even from the same source.

The legal side matters more than people usually think. Using a recognizable excerpt generally requires clearance from both the master rights holder and the publishing rights holder; otherwise, a claim can follow. Some producers negotiate a sample fee or royalty share, while others rely on licenses or short uses that are unlikely to be challenged. I have always found the clearance process odd: the person who made the original song is often not the person holding the rights, so a new producer may be negotiating with a label or a rights administrator. That gap between artistic use and legal ownership is why some samples get cleared, while others get pulled from albums. A familiar example is The Prodigy's Firestarter, which repurposes a Human League vocal into an electronic beat.

I also think sampling works best when the old recording is used as reference rather than quote. If a producer borrows a drum break or a bass line, enough of the sound needs to be recognisable, without letting the original overwhelm the new track. That balance is where the craft shows. Sampling is a way of arguing with the past, taking what was already recorded and making it do something different.

My own position is that this makes sampling one of the most interesting forms of modern music writing. It turns a finished song into material for a new argument. When done well, the original remains audible but no longer in its old context, and the listener can feel the connection without being pulled back into the older recording.

I don’t think the brain itself hurts, at least not directly. The brain has few pain receptors, so a headache is mostly pain in the structures around it: the scalp, the meninges, the sinuses, and blood vessels. In tension headaches, the muscles and fascia around the head tighten, and that pull is felt as a band-like pressure. In migraines, the trigeminal nerve becomes sensitized, often with vasodilation and inflammatory mediators, which makes nearby nerves and membranes more reactive. My own headaches feel less like a fixed spot and more like the whole system turning up the volume: nerves reporting threat, muscles tensing, vessels changing tone. I have noticed that when I skip a meal, the pressure returns, and eating and resting reduce it, and it eases within minutes. That is why the same pressure can feel different depending on whether it is stress, dehydration, a cold, or a migraine.

I couldn’t even tell you if the food was good because we never got to eat. We got there Sunday at 7:20 p.m. and picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it would be easy. We put our names on their completely useless digital waitlist, then were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15. Just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait runs that far past payment, tell people up front so our night isn’t completely wasted. Absolute disaster; zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn't offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either; it reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any. I'd call this buffet acceptable, but it's really overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider going again.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace again. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I am typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for the postage and boxing it up, and I would have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life; well, the under-21 version, and have sat through plenty of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too: the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil, not in a rip-off way exactly, just comparable feats with maybe more clarity. Clarity is the problem. As a long-time visitor, the story bit really bothered me, actually. What is the story? A dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing: more must be better, so they crammed everything in. Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. The shirts never arrived because the sales representative transcribed our delivery address wrongly: her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. The intended address was 5407, but the package went to 5401. The residents there brought it to the local UPS store for return. Then the package disappeared and was never seen again. We did not find out until several weeks later. In the middle of the dispute we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original pair. The owner handled the matter at that stage. He admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong address, but said no refund unless the shirts were returned. He suggested we were partly to blame for not being friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and we eventually got a credit.
